answers.brief_reasoning: Ionic solid: cations and anions in a lattice held by electrostatic attraction.
answers.final_answer: NaCl is made of Na⁺ cations and Cl⁻ anions arranged in a 3-D crystal lattice. Strong electrostatic (Coulombic) attractions between the oppositely charged ions, i.e. ionic bonds, hold them in place.

answers.brief_reasoning: Solid NaCl has ions fixed in the lattice, so it does not conduct. Molten or dissolved, the ions can move, so it conducts. SiO₂ has neither ions nor delocalized electrons, so it does not conduct in any state.
answers.final_answer: As solids, neither conducts well. In solid NaCl the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are locked in the lattice and cannot move. SiO₂ is an insulator: all its valence electrons are held in localized Si–O covalent bonds and it contains no ions. When NaCl is melted or dissolved in water, its ions can move and carry charge, so it conducts. Molten SiO₂ still has no mobile charged particles, so it does not conduct. Overall, NaCl can conduct (when molten or in solution) and SiO₂ cannot.
answers.flaw_note: The prompt doesn't say which state (solid, molten or dissolved) to compare, so the answer covers both.

answers.brief_reasoning: To melt SiO₂ you have to break strong covalent bonds throughout the network.
answers.final_answer: SiO₂ has the higher melting point (about 1700 °C, compared with about 801 °C for NaCl). Melting SiO₂ means breaking many strong Si–O covalent bonds that run through the whole 3-D network. These take more energy to overcome than the ionic attractions between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.

answers.brief_reasoning: Boiling point goes up from HCl (188 K) to HBr (206 K) to HI (237 K). Molar mass and the number of electrons also go up in that order, so the electron cloud gets larger and more polarizable. That makes the London dispersion forces stronger, and more energy is needed to separate the molecules. Dipole-dipole forces actually get weaker down the group because the polarity decreases, so the dispersion forces must be what controls the trend.
answers.final_answer: Boiling point increases HCl < HBr < HI because larger, more polarizable electron clouds give stronger London dispersion forces.

answers.brief_reasoning: HF molecules hydrogen-bond to each other because H is bonded directly to F, which is very electronegative and small. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than the dipole-dipole and dispersion forces in HCl and HBr. They outweigh HF's weaker dispersion forces, so HF has a much higher boiling point.
answers.final_answer: HF has strong hydrogen bonding between molecules; HCl and HBr do not.

answers.brief_reasoning: HF's normal boiling point (293 K) is far above HCl's (188 K), so HF has stronger intermolecular forces. At 250 K, HF is below its boiling point, so its vapor pressure is less than 1 atm. HCl is above its boiling point, so its vapor pressure would be more than 1 atm. Therefore HF has the lower vapor pressure.
answers.final_answer: The vapor pressure of HF is lower than that of HCl at 250 K.
